Abstract:
The application of computer vision and machine learning methods for semantic segmentation of the structural elements of 3D-printed products in the field of additive manufacturing (AM) can improve real-time failure analysis systems and potentially reduce the number of defects by providing additional tools for in situ corrections. This work demonstrates the possibilities of using physics-based rendering for labeled image dataset generation, as well as image-to-image style transfer capabilities to improve the accuracy of real image segmentation for AM systems. Multi-class semantic segmentation experiments were carried out based on the U-Net model and the cycle generative adversarial network. The test results demonstrated the capacity of this method to detect such structural elements of 3D-printed parts as a top (last printed) layer, infill, shell, and support. A basis for further segmentation system enhancement by utilizing image-to-image style transfer and domain adaptation technologies was also considered. The results indicate that using style transfer as a precursor to domain adaptation can improve real 3D printing image segmentation in situations where a model trained on synthetic data is the only tool available. The mean intersection over union (mIoU) scores for synthetic test datasets included 94.90% for the entire 3D-printed part, 73.33% for the top layer, 78.93% for the infill, 55.31% for the shell, and 69.45% for supports.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ensuring real-time quality assurance in additive manufacturing (AM), particularly Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM), is essential due to its widespread adoption across industries driven by its process efficiency, design flexibility, and low material waste. However, conventional defect detection methods exhibit fundamental limitations in capturing spatially distributed and subtle surface anomalies. These limitations stem from their localized receptive fields and strong inductive biases, which restrict their ability to generalize to complex surface patterns. To address these challenges, this study proposes an explicitly optimized method based on Vision Transformers (ViTs) for real-time surface anomaly detection in the FDM process. We evaluate four surface conditions (normal, under-extrusion, over-extrusion, and void/empty regions) and generate explainability outputs on-demand to preserve real-time monitoring. Unlike CNNs, ViTs utilize global self-attention mechanisms, enabling them to capture long-range dependencies and subtle spatial variations across the printed surface. This methodological advantage allows for enhanced sensitivity to defect characteristics that conventional models often overlook. The method integrates depth maps derived from 2D laser scanning to construct high-fidelity surface topology representations, facilitating accurate classification of key defect types, including under-extrusion, over-extrusion, voids, and normal printing. To support practical deployment, we include post-hoc explanation modules based on attention visualization, gradient-based attribution (Integrated Gradients/ Saliency), and embedding-space projection (t-SNE and UMAP) to provide operator-facing evidence of regions and representation structure associated with each prediction. Experimental evaluation achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.877 and a macro-averaged mean AUC (mAUC) of 0.972, with an inference latency of 14.80–32.45 ms per patch, supporting real-time layer-wise inspection. Together, this work delivers a practical solution for surface quality monitoring, representing a significant advancement in intelligent quality assurance for AM processes.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The persistent challenge of adhesion in Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) technology is deeply rooted in the mechanical and chemical properties of utilized materials, necessitating the exploration of potential resolutions. This involves adjustments targeting the interplay of printing parameters, the mechanical fortification of print beds, and the integration of more adhesive materials, resonating across user levels, from enthusiasts to complex industrial configurations. An in-depth investigation is outlined in this paper, detailing the plan for a systematically designed device. Engineered for FFF device installation, the device facilitates the detachment of printed models, while precisely recording the detachment process, capturing the maximum force, and its progression over time. The primary objective is fabricating a comprehensive measurement apparatus, created for adhesion assessment. The device is adaptable across diverse FFF machines and print bed typologies, conforming to pre-defined conditions, with key features including compactness, facile manipulability, and capacity for recurrent measurements. This pursuit involves evaluating adhesion levels in prints made from diverse materials on varying print bed compositions, aiming to establish a comprehensive database. This repository facilitates judicious material and bed type selection, emphasizing maximal compatibility. Emphasis is placed on operating within a thermally stable context, a pivotal prerequisite for consistent and reproducible results.

Abstract:
The adoption of Additive Manufacturing (AM) has gradually transformed the fashion industry through innovation and technology over the last decade. Novel AM systems and techniques are continuously being developed, leading to the application of AM polymers with textiles and fabrics in the fashion industry. This work investigates the development and testing of polymer–textile composites using polylactic acid (PLA) filaments on synthetic mesh fabrics using direct material extrusion (ME). An aspect of this paper highlights the appropriate combination of printing material, textile substrate, and printer settings to achieve excellent polymer–textile adhesion. Details of the printing process to create polymer–textile composites are described, as are the interfacial strength results of the T-peel tests, and the observed failure modes post-testing. The peel strengths for different ME bonded polymer–textile composites are examined and used to identify the compatibility of materials. This work visualised the potential of direct ME of polymers onto textile fabrics as a material-joining approach for new textile functionalisation, multi-material composite explorations and innovative aesthetic print techniques. This work also adds to the limited knowledge of AM polymer–textile composites, which can provide helpful information for designers and researchers to develop new applications and facilitate future research development in smart embedded and programmable textiles.

Abstract:
<jats:p>3D-printed polymers and polymer composites are increasingly used in sliding and abrasive contacts, but their friction and wear cannot be transferred directly from data for moulded polymers, because printing creates layered interfaces, process-specific surface textures and position-dependent crystallinity. This systematised critical review analyses 289 experimental studies and grades the evidence for each step linking the printing process to internal structure, surface, contact conditions, wear mechanisms and component life. Four findings stand out. First, the orientation of layers and rasters relative to sliding is associated with a switch between wear controlled by shear of interlayer bonds and wear controlled by crossing of surface ridges; coding orientation as {contact face, layer normal, raster/fibre direction} explains several apparently contradictory results. Second, test conditions dominate absolute wear rates, which for printed neat PEEK span 2.6 decades, with the largest contrast between contact configurations, so effects must be compared within studies. Third, only 3 of 245 full-text studies report all core contact and statistical information; a minimum reporting set is proposed. Fourth, only three printed-versus-conventional comparisons isolate the manufacturing route. Established findings include the failure of hardness as a general wear predictor and friction reduction by oil and grease; lubricant storage in designed porosity remains probable.</jats:p>

Abstract:

 Peel adhesion properties of 3D-printed tactile graphics on Bond paper were evaluated in this study to determine the durability and bonding strength of various print materials. The tactile graphics were manufactured using the Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) technique on an Ender 3 pro printer. Four different thermoplastic materials such as Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), Polylactic acid (PLA), Polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), and Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) were used for printing, with all models sliced in cure software using consistent print settings. An adhesion enhancement feature specifically the brim adhesion layer, was applied to improve bonding between the material and the bond paper substrate. The peel adhesion test was conducted using a customized approach, wherein each sample was evaluated at three equidistant points to ensure uniformity in data collection, and the average peel strength was calculated. The results indicated that the PETG with the adhesion layer exhibited the highest bonding strength, achieving a peel force of 5.02N, while PLA with an adhesion layer demonstrated consistent and stable performance throughout the testing process. In contrast, TPU recorded the lowest adhesion strength at 0.84N, suggesting limited bonding efficiency strong adhesion and a smooth surface finish strong adhesion and a smooth surface finish with bond paper. ABS showed intermediate performance in both adhesion strength and print reliability. PLA and PETG also excelled in terms of print quality, dimensional stability, and process consistency. To assess the statistical significance of the difference among materials, one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was applied, followed by Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test for pairwise comparison. These findings provide critical insights into material selection for producing durable, high-quality tactile graphics suitable for assistive applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Three-dimensional printed polymers produced using Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM) exhibit directional microstructures resulting from filament paths, layer interfaces, and cellular infill, leading to mechanical and tribological responses distinct from those of homogeneous bulk materials. This study presents a comparative tribomechanical evaluation of polypropylene (PP) bulk inserts and 3D-printed polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG) inserts with a 30% hexagonal infill, relevant for robotic gripping applications. Progressive scratch tests were performed under loads from 5 to 100 N (150 N for PP), and profilometry was applied to quantify groove morphology, ridge formation, and displaced-volume ratios. An elasto-plastic conical indentation model was used to derive indentation pressures and elastic–plastic transition radii from groove geometry. The PETG inserts exhibited heterogeneous groove depth, intermittent ridge tearing, and friction fluctuations associated with the internal infill structure, consistent with previous findings on anisotropy and architecture-dependent behaviour in additively manufactured polymers. In contrast, bulk PP demonstrated smoother friction profiles and more stable plastic flow under increasing loads. Two functional indices—specific frictional work and ridge-to-trace volumetric ratio—are introduced to support material selection for robotic gripping systems. The results show that local contact mechanics in 3D-printed inserts are governed by print-induced structural features and can be effectively evaluated through a scratch-based elasto-plastic analysis. The methods and results presented in this work support the rational selection and design of polymer inserts for robotic gripper fingertips. The proposed scratch-based elasto-plastic evaluation framework enables manufacturers and automation engineers to compare 3D-printed and conventional materials based on friction stability, wear response, and deformation resistance. This approach can be directly applied to optimise gripping performance in industrial handling, packaging, and collaborative robotics.</jats:p>

<jats:p>PETG composite filaments containing 1 wt%, 3 wt%, and 5 wt% hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) were produced. The produced filaments were transformed into test specimens using the fused deposition modeling (FDM) technique. The tensile, compression, and wear behaviors of the composite polymer test specimens produced by the FDM method were investigated. The wear characteristic was measured using a ball-on-flat tribometer under normal loads of 5, 10, and 15 N. The worn surfaces were characterized by profilometer, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX). PETG/1hBN showed the lowest coefficient of friction (COF) at all tested loads and provided a 40–46% reduction compared to neat PETG. These results show that the addition of a low amount of h-BN to PETG is an effective and easily processable method for improving the wear resistance of the PETG matrix.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Additive manufacturing, commonly known as 3D printing, is an advancement over traditional formative manufacturing methods. It can increase efficiency in manufacturing operations highlighting advantages such as rapid prototyping, reduction of waste, reduction of manufacturing time and cost, and increased flexibility in a production setting. The additive manufacturing (AM) process consists of five steps: (1) preparation of 3D models for printing (designing the part/object), (2) conversion to STL file, (3) slicing and setting of 3D printing parameters, (4) actual printing, and (5) finishing/post-processing methods. Very often, the 3D printed part is sufficient by itself without further post-printing processing. However, many applications still require some forms of post-processing, especially those for industrial applications. This review focuses on the importance of different finishing/post-processing methods for 3D-printed polymers. Different 3D printing technologies and materials are considered in presenting the authors’ perspective. The advantages and disadvantages of using these methods are also discussed together with the cost and time in doing the post-processing activities. Lastly, this review also includes discussions on the enhancement of properties such as electrical, mechanical, and chemical, and other characteristics such as geometrical precision, durability, surface properties, and aesthetic value with post-printing processing. Future perspectives is also provided towards the end of this review.

The excerpt describes an automated build-plate removal system based on flexing/raising a magnetic removable bed, powered rollers, and passive scraping. Because the Prusa magnetic bed could not be pulled directly from the front, an elevator first breaks the magnetic retention and raises the bed 52 mm; rollers then feed it into a bending track. The selected lead-screw stepper motors could provide 122 N and had a maximum torque of 0.04 N·m, versus a calculated initial lifting torque of 5.91 × 10^-3 N·m. This instrumentation measured and recorded tensile force over time during detachment, providing the basis for adhesion-force measurements. Testing was conducted using a Prusa Mk3s+ printer and four types of bed materials. In the supplied passage, the tested model is explicitly identified as PETG; no PLA-specific measurement results or numerical adhesion forces are provided. Abstract:
This paper presents a conceptual design and implementation of a soft, compliant 3D printed gripper (SurgGrip), conceived for automated grasping of various surgery-based thin-flat instruments. The proposed solution includes (1) a gripper with a resilient mechanism to increase safety and better adaptation to the unstructured environment; (2) flat fingertips with mortise and tenon joint to facilitate pinching and enveloping based grasping of thin and random shape tools; (3) a soft pad on the fingertips to enable the high surface area to maintain stable grasping of the surgical instruments; (4) a four-bar linkage with a leadscrew mechanism to provide a precise finger movement; (5) enable automated manipulation of surgical tools using computer vision. Our gripper model is designed and fabricated by integrating soft and rigid components through a hybrid approach. The SurgGrip shows passive adaptation through inherent compliance of linear and torsional spring. The four-bar linkage mechanism controlled by a motor–leadscrew–nut drive provides precise gripper opening and closing movements. The experimental results show that the SurgGrip can detect, segment through a camera, and grasp surgical instruments (maximum 606.73 gs), with a 67% success rate (grasped 10 out of 12 selected tools) at 3.21 mm/s grasping speed and 15.81 s object grasping time autonomously. Besides, we demonstrated the pick and place abilities of SurgGrip on flat and nonflat surfaces in real-time.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The increasing demand for flexible, high-precision, and low-damage manufacturing is driving industrial robotic grippers toward adaptive systems with compliant interaction, force regulation, and intelligent decision-making capabilities. However, their industrial deployment remains limited by three major challenges: the trade-off between structural compliance and load-bearing capability, the insufficient coordination between sensing performance and closed-loop force control, and the limited generalization and safety validation of learning-based methods. This review presents an engineering-oriented analysis of adaptive robotic grippers based on three paradigms: structural compliance, active compliance, and learning-enabled grasping. The design principles, performance characteristics, and application limitations of compliant mechanisms, variable stiffness structures, carbon fiber composites, embedded sensing, force control, data-driven methods, reinforcement learning, and model–data fusion are discussed. A comparative framework is established according to the adaptation mechanisms, key parameters, performance boundaries, and industrial applications. The analysis shows that representative underactuated grippers typically achieve 3–19 degrees of freedom, grasping success rates of 90–98%, and load capacities of approximately 10–50 N, but remain limited in force regulation. Actively compliant grippers achieve force errors of 0.1–1 N, position errors of 0.05–0.5 mm, and control frequencies of 500 Hz–1 kHz, while learning-enabled methods require 102–104 samples for compensation and 105–106 interactions for reinforcement learning. The model–data fusion provides a practical balance between adaptability, interpretability, and safety. Future adaptive grippers will evolve toward integrated structure, sensing, learning, and control architectures with enhanced reliability and industrial applicability.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Abstract The demand for flexible grasping of various objects by robotic hands in the industry is rapidly growing. To address this, we propose a novel variable stiffness gripper (VSG). The VSG design is based on a parallel-guided beam structure inserted by a slider from one end, allowing stiffness variation by changing the length of the parallel beams participating in the system. This design enables continuous adjustment between high compliance and high stiffness of the gripper fingers, providing robustness through its mechanical structure. The linear analytical model of the deflection and stiffness of the parallel beam is derived, which is suitable for small and medium deflections. The contribution of each parameter of the parallel beam to the stiffness is analyzed and discussed. Also, a prototype of the VSG is developed, achieving a stiffness ratio of 70.9, which is highly competitive. Moreover, a vision-based force sensing method utilizing ArUco markers is proposed as a replacement for traditional force sensors. By this method, the VSG is capable of closed-loop control during the grasping process, ensuring efficiency and safety under a well-defined grasping strategy framework. Experimental tests are conducted to emphasize the importance and safety of stiffness variation. In addition, it shows the high performance of the VSG in adaptive grasping for asymmetric scenarios and its ability to flexible grasping for objects with various hardness and fragility. These findings provide new insights for future developments in the field of variable stiffness grippers.

Abstract:
As there come to be more applications of intelligent robots, their task object is becoming more varied. However, it is still a challenge for a robot to handle unfamiliar objects. We review the recent work on the feature sensing and robotic grasping of objects with uncertain information. In particular, we focus on how the robot perceives the features of an object, so as to reduce the uncertainty of objects, and how the robot completes object grasping through the learning-based approach when the traditional approach fails. The uncertain information is classified into geometric information and physical information. Based on the type of uncertain information, the object is further classified into three categories, which are geometric-uncertain objects, physical-uncertain objects, and unknown objects. Furthermore, the approaches to the feature sensing and robotic grasping of these objects are presented based on the varied characteristics of each type of object. Finally, we summarize the reviewed approaches for uncertain objects and provide some interesting issues to be more investigated in the future. It is found that the object’s features, such as material and compactness, are difficult to be sensed, and the object grasping approach based on learning networks plays a more important role when the unknown degree of the task object increases.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Precision grasping is a fundamental capability for dexterous robotic manipulation, enabling robots to handle small objects, perform delicate tasks, and interact safely with complex environments. However, achieving stable and accurate fingertip control remains challenging due to mechanical complexity, actuation limitations, and sensing constraints. This paper presents a comprehensive review of robotic hand designs from the perspective of precision grasping. The review analyzes key aspects of mechanical architecture, including finger kinematic structures, actuation and transmission systems, structural materials and fabrication methods, mechanical intelligence, and control-oriented mechanical design. Different design strategies such as fully actuated fingers, underactuated mechanisms, tendon-driven systems, linkage-based architectures, and soft robotic structures are compared in terms of dexterity, adaptability, accuracy, and system complexity. The analysis highlights several important trends, including the transition toward compliant and bio-inspired mechanisms, the integration of lightweight materials and additive manufacturing, and the increasing role of sensor–structure integration for precise force and position control. Despite significant progress, challenges such as friction, hysteresis, transmission compliance, and limited integration space still affect grasping accuracy and reliability. Based on the reviewed literature, future research should focus on hybrid actuation strategies, bio-inspired structural design, graded material architectures with structurally integrated sensing, and modular platforms to improve precision manipulation and system robustness in next-generation robotic hands.</jats:p>

Abstract:
To achieve high-accuracy grasping of unknown objects, we present novel multilevel convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for robotic grasping with a parallel gripper or multifingered dexterous hand. The multilevel CNNs include four levels with different structures and functions. The first level is constructed to get the approximate position of the grasped object. The second level aims to obtain the preselected grasping rectangles. The third level is constructed to re-evaluate the preselected grasping rectangles and obtain substantially detailed features with quite a large network, so as to assess each preselected grasping rectangle exactly. By using a selection algorithm, the optimal grasping rectangle can be determined and unknown object grasping can be achieved with a parallel gripper. The purpose of the fourth level is to obtain the finger position distribution to complete the accurate grasping of unknown objects with a multifingered dexterous hand. The test results indicate that, compared to state-of-the-art methods, the proposed multilevel CNNs can greatly increase the precision of the grasping rectangle. Grasping experiments were implemented on a Youbot arm with five degrees of freedom and a Shadow four-fingered dexterous hand. The results show that the multilevel CNNs can determine the optimal grasping rectangle and finger position distribution, thereby achieving high-accuracy grasping of various unknown objects, even under several complex environmental conditions.Note to Practitioners—Robot grasping of objects lags far behind human experiences and poses a significant challenge in the robotics area. To solve it, we present new multilevel convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to process red green blue-depth (RGB-D) images and realize optimal grasping detection of unknown objects. Moreover, we provide details of the network structure, network training, and network testing. The testing results obtained from the open grasping data set show that the multilevel CNNs can significantly increase the accuracy of the grasping rectangle compared to state-of-the-art methods. Experiments were implemented on different robotic platforms, including a five-degrees-of-freedom Youbot arm with a parallel gripper and a UR5 robot arm with a Shadow multifingered dexterous hand. The results validate that the multilevel CNNs offer excellent generalization and robustness for handling different sizes and shapes of unknown objects, as well as background disturbances, which are key problems in robotic manipulation.

Abstract:
For robust grasping of workpieces with complex surface geometries such as the plugs of electrical connectors (ECs), individually designed gripper jaws are commonly required. The manual design of the latter is time-consuming, iterative, expensive, and requires expert knowledge. Therefore, automating the design process offers the potential to increase efficiency and reduce costs. However, the plugs of ECs often involve interference contours which pose a high risk for a grasp to fail. Thus, this paper introduces an approach for the automated design of gripper jaws that considers complex surface geometries with interference contours. Thereby, expected geometric uncertainties in the relative pose between a plug and a gripper system can be parameterized by a user. The key steps of our approach are to automatically simulate collision volumes between the gripper jaws and the workpiece to map geometric uncertainties in software for computer-aided design (CAD) and to adapt the gripper jaws accordingly within minutes and without manual design. The results of the experimental validation using three different high-voltage plugs show that the presented approach is suitable for robust grasping of such workpieces. In summary, our work intends to contribute to a more efficient design process of gripper systems for workpieces with complex surface geometries such as plugs of ECs.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The rapid advancement and expanding application of robotics in various sectors necessitate the development of versatile and efficient gripping systems. Robotic grippers, serving as the primary interface between robots and the physical world, are pivotal for the success of robotic applications ranging from industrial automation to delicate tasks in healthcare. This paper delves into the diverse landscape of robotic grippers, examining their design principles, material choices, and the intricate balance between flexibility and strength required to cater to a broad spectrum of operational demands. It further explores the spectrum of actuation mechanisms that empower these grippers, from traditional electric and pneumatic systems to cutting-edge soft robotics technologies that offer unprecedented adaptability and safety. The integration of sensors within grippers, enhancing their intelligence and autonomy, is also scrutinized, alongside a critical evaluation of control strategies that range from conventional PID controllers to sophisticated machine learning algorithms. The aim of this comprehensive review is not only to provide a foundational understanding of the current state of robotic gripper technology but also to highlight key considerations and emerging trends that will shape the future of robotic manipulation. Through this exploration, the paper seeks to equip designers, engineers, and researchers with the insights needed to innovate and advance the field of robotic gripping systems.</jats:p>

ATCAM ejects each printed dynamic coupon using an in situ actuator (ISA) integrated into the printer setup. The coupon is designed as a sphere with a specially shaped base that provides a reliable deployment surface. The base includes a cavity that reduces the area contacting the build plate and therefore lowers the force needed for ejection. After deployment, the actuator sends the coupon along a trajectory toward an acrylic target attached to the load cell, where its impact is measured. The system is then able to reuse the cleared build surface to print and eject the next coupon. The actuator is described as generating 2 N of force, and the coupon geometry was selected for reliable deployment within that force limit. ## pqac-00000058

From text 'me2020increasing3dprinter pages 1-7'.

PR ME. Increasing 3d printer throughput with automated part removal. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt provides a qualitative comparison between manual and automated 3D-print-farm operation, but it does not report numerical throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, labor cost, or cost-per-part measurements. In the manual workflow, an operator must remove each completed print and start the next job; this creates downtime and makes printer throughput dependent on operator availability and performance. The proposed automated system uses a print queue in OctoPrint on a Raspberry Pi. After a print finishes, it removes the part by flexing a removable bed through a curved track, returns the bed to the printer, and starts the next queued job. For printers without removable beds, a clamping mechanism and custom removable bed are used. The intended benefits are continuous operation, reduced cycle-to-cycle downtime, reduced direct human involvement, and the ability to manage multiple jobs in succession. Testing showed successful full removal cycles without human interaction, while longer-duration overnight, weekend, and full-filament-spool tests were identified as future reliability tests rather than reported results. The system is designed to be modular and scalable across multiple printers. Therefore, the excerpt supports the expectation of improved uptime and lower operator hours per print compared with manual operation, but provides no data for calculating or comparing actual throughput, labor savings, or per-part costs.

## pqac-00000059

From text 'dizon2021postprocessingof3dprinted pages 28-29'.

John Ryan C. Dizon, Ciara Catherine L. Gache, Honelly Mae S. Cascolan, Lina T. Cancino, and Rigoberto C. Advincula. Post-processing of 3d-printed polymers. Technologies, 9:61, Aug 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies9030061, doi:10.3390/technologies9030061. This article has 319 citations.

The excerpt is relevant to comparing manual and automated 3D-printing-farm operations, particularly for post-processing rather than printer uptime itself. Manual post-processing can be difficult to scale, adds labor and processing time, and may introduce quality-control problems. Reported labor costs are approximately USD 30–100 per hour, while post-processing can add roughly 17%–100% to the original printing time on a batch basis. These additions directly affect human-hours per print, throughput, and cost per part. The article estimates that post-processing may account for about 30% of the manufacturing cost of a printed part, and cites a 26% finishing/post-processing share for metal or polymer parts. Automation is presented as necessary for minimizing labor and time costs, especially in production environments. For a farm-level comparison, the excerpt supports measuring manual versus automated workflows by labor hours per part, added processing time, total cost per part, and whether finishing can keep pace with printer output. It also emphasizes that post-processing should not negate additive manufacturing’s advantages over molded or formed parts. However, the excerpt does not provide direct numerical values for printer uptime, farm utilization, automated cycle times, or complete per-part economics, so those metrics would require additional sources or operational data.

## pqac-00000060

From text 'me2020increasing3dprinter pages 19-23'.

PR ME. Increasing 3d printer throughput with automated part removal. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt supports a qualitative comparison of manual and automated 3D-printing-farm operations, but it does not provide a numerical throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, or cost-per-part calculation. A print may take several hours, while preparation through slicing generally takes no more than fifteen minutes. In manual operation, the printer remains unavailable after a print finishes until a worker removes the part, resets the machine, and starts the next job. This creates downtime and lowers effective uptime and throughput. Continuous operation requires a person or team to repeatedly clear completed parts and launch new prints, increasing labor demand and operating cost. The text characterizes this labor as expensive and inefficient, particularly in high-throughput environments such as print farms. It also notes that printing can run in the background, reducing active operator involvement during production, although the need for manual removal remains the bottleneck. Automated part removal is therefore presented as a way to reduce the idle interval between prints, decrease required human intervention, and increase printer utilization and farm throughput. Exact cost savings or productivity improvements would require additional data, including print duration, changeover time, labor rates, failure rates, number of printers, and the performance of the proposed automated system.

From text 'me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9'.

PR ME. Increasing 3d printer throughput with automated part removal. Unknown journal, 2020.

The excerpt describes an automated 3D-printer part-removal system intended to increase print-farm uptime and reduce the need for continuous manual intervention. Reliability testing involves initiating and removing prints continuously, including operation overnight, over a weekend, and through an entire 1 kg spool of PLA filament. Successful operation for the full spool is described as the system’s maximum efficiency, because a human operator would then only need to replace the filament spool every few days. The system supports sequential production of the same part, making a group of printers more suitable for mass production, and can scale across a print farm by adding a removal system to each printer. It also supports queued production of different parts, helping organize complete assemblies. However, this excerpt does not provide numerical throughput, uptime percentage, labor hours per print, cost per part, labor savings, or a direct quantitative comparison between automated and manual operations. It establishes the intended operational benefits—longer unattended runtime, reduced operator availability requirements, repeated production, scalability, and print queuing—but additional sections or experimental results would be needed to calculate throughput, human-hours per part, and cost per part.

## pqac-00000066

From text 'yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12'.

Won-Jae Yun, Sungjin Hong, Kyu-Wha Lee, Dohyeon Kim, Hyungjung Kim, and Sung-Hoon Ahn. Smartlab: flexible and interoperable manufacturing laboratory system for remote education and research using a mobile manipulator. J. Comput. Des. Eng., 12:221-235, Mar 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1093/jcde/qwaf034, doi:10.1093/jcde/qwaf034. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt documents a SmartLab remote-education pilot conducted from SNU in South Korea for 21 students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania. Students remotely controlled or observed automated material-testing experiments, with GUI control and real-time 360° VR streaming. The system remained operational despite temporary network disconnections; when real-time monitoring was interrupted, recorded VR video could be replayed to review the experiment. This supports robustness and continuity, but the excerpt does not report a numerical job-completion rate. For turnaround, SmartLab required an average of 17 minutes to handle one specimen, excluding fabrication, compared with 9 minutes for a human researcher. Despite the slower per-specimen cycle, its automation produced a theoretical monthly capacity of 664 specimens versus 252 for human researchers. The main intervention described was manual battery charging: the robot’s battery lasted eight experimental cycles, after which human researchers had to recharge it because no automatic charging dock was available. The excerpt contains no information about remote cloud-lab users submitting design-print-test jobs, the BEAR external-user pilot, or separate teleoperated test laboratories. Thus, it provides evidence primarily for the Tanzania pilot, resilience to network interruptions, turnaround time, throughput, and the need for periodic human battery intervention.

## pqac-00000067

From text 'yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 13-13'.

Won-Jae Yun, Sungjin Hong, Kyu-Wha Lee, Dohyeon Kim, Hyungjung Kim, and Sung-Hoon Ahn. Smartlab: flexible and interoperable manufacturing laboratory system for remote education and research using a mobile manipulator. J. Comput. Des. Eng., 12:221-235, Mar 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1093/jcde/qwaf034, doi:10.1093/jcde/qwaf034. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt provides evidence about the SmartLab Tanzania remote-education demonstration, but it does not discuss the BEAR external-user pilot, remote cloud-lab users submitting design-print-test jobs, or teleoperated test laboratories in general. In Tanzania, students remotely performed material-testing experiments despite limited technological infrastructure and unstable network conditions. They used SmartLab’s remote-control interface and real-time monitoring tools, demonstrating the feasibility of remote laboratory education in locations without direct access to advanced equipment. VR streaming was also identified as a way to improve engagement and make remote experiments more interactive. {"answer": "## Robotic Part Removal, Closed-Loop Design-Print-Test Systems, and Supporting Technologies for FFF/FDM 3D Printing Automation

### (1) Academic and Industrial Systems for Robotic Part Removal from FFF/FDM Printers

The following table compares all identified systems:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**BEAR / MAMA BEAR (Boston University).** The Bayesian Experimental Autonomous Researcher (BEAR), first reported in Gongora et al. 2020 (*Science Advances*, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aaz1708), uses five dual-extruder MakerGear M3 FDM printers arranged within the working radius of a six-axis Universal Robots UR5e arm, a Sartorius CP225D scale, and an Instron 5965 universal testing machine (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). The expanded campaign (Snapp et al. 2024, *Nature Communications*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48534-4) details the removal method: before each print, an arm-mounted camera checks whether the bed is clear; if cleaning is needed, the arm uses a scraper with up to ten retry attempts, taking a verification photo each time; if the bed remains dirty the printer is deactivated and an operator is notified (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). After printing, the bed is heated for TPE and TPU-1/2 (100 °C) to facilitate removal, or allowed to cool to 30 °C for PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3 (pqac-00000041). Failure modes include dirty beds, unsuccessful component grabs, misorientation, mass/height deviations >5%, severe print defects, insufficient strain data, and periodic need to replace worn polyimide tape and load new filament rolls (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). No explicit handling success-rate percentage was reported.

**FlexTrak automated sheet-flexing system (thesis, 2020).** This non-peer-reviewed student project describes a modular system for the Prusa i3 MK3 that elevates the magnetic spring-steel sheet off the bed (requiring approximately 15.48 N normal force to break magnetic retention, and 6.76 N horizontal pull), feeds it through a curved bending track using powered rollers, and uses passive scrapers to remove remaining debris (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). A decision-matrix comparison rated sheet flexing higher than disposable roll media (3.75 vs. 3.1) for reliability, modularity, and maintainability (pqac-00000018). Scraper-only removal was tested and found unreliable: it damaged small parts, retained parts on the blade, was limited to about 38% of the bed area (150 cm² maximum on a 400 cm² bed), required favorable part orientation and rafts, and produced visible scrape marks after 250 cycles (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022). Print-head collision/ejection was also described, wherein modified G-code causes the print head to ram the part off; this requires no hardware modification but needs parts approximately 1 inch tall and becomes harder as contact area increases (pqac-00000017). Overnight, weekend, and full-spool reliability tests were planned but not quantitatively reported (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

**ATCAM (Mazhari et al. 2021, *Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance*, DOI: 10.1007/s11665-021-06042-2).** This peer-reviewed system prints dynamic coupons on a Prusa MK3S and ejects them using an in-situ actuator (ISA) printed on the build surface; the toolhead pulls back the ISA, which releases stored energy through a 25.4 mm sphere to impact-eject each coupon toward a load cell (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). The actuator generates approximately 2 N of force, and the coupon base is designed with reduced contact area to lower adhesion. Each ISA was reused for 100 nondestructive ejection cycles, after which manual replacement was required (pqac-00000045). A total of 3,000 coupons were generated across three PLA feedstocks (pqac-00000048). No explicit ejection success rate was reported, but automated ejection was described as the most difficult engineering challenge (pqac-00000044).

**SmartLab (Yun et al. 2025, *Journal of Computational Design and Engineering*, DOI: 10.1093/jcde/qwaf034).** This peer-reviewed system uses a San Robotics M1013 arm on a Syscon Scorpion A-100 mobile base. After printing, the robot removes the entire printer bed with a suction gripper, measures the specimen with a wrist camera, changes to a finger gripper via a pneumatic gripper changer, detaches the specimen, and places it on a rack for downstream measurement and testing (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000012). No bed temperature or cool-down protocol was specified in the retrieved evidence.

**Commercial systems.** Prusa Research's automated farm system (Prusa Pro AFS) and other commercial plate-swapping solutions (e.g., Bambu Lab conveyor concepts) exist as trade products, but **no peer-reviewed trial counts, success rates, failure-mode studies, or comparative cost analyses were located.** These should be treated as commercial/trade sources only.

### (2) Closed-Loop Design-Print-Test Systems with Robotic Specimen Handling

**BEAR (2020) and MAMA BEAR / expanded campaign (2024)** are the most extensively documented systems. BEAR demonstrated fully autonomous closed-loop operation: Bayesian optimization selected a structure design, OpenSCAD generated the STL, Slic3r produced G-code, OctoPrint managed the printer, the UR5e retrieved the part, weighed it, loaded it into the Instron 5965, and the compression test result fed back into Gaussian-process regression to guide the next experiment (pqac-00000004). In the original campaign, 600 designs were tested in triplicate without human intervention; 32 experiments in 12 hours matched a 1,800-experiment grid campaign, and 64 experiments in 24 hours exceeded it (pqac-00000006). The expanded campaign reported 25,387 experiments across seven materials (TPE, TPU-1/NinjaFlex, TPU-2/Cheetah, TPU-3/Armadillo, Nylon, PETG, PLA), with experiments running approximately 60% of wall-clock time and each mechanical test taking approximately 10 minutes (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000039). This directly contradicts any claim that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop. Human interventions included periodic manual bed cleaning when automated scraping failed after ten attempts, filament replacement, and polyimide tape maintenance (pqac-00000038). The authors state limitations including manufacturing variability (mass CV 4.6%, toughness CV 12.8%) and the need for human monitoring to modify campaign parameters during the multi-year operation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000040).

**SmartLab (2025)** demonstrated a closed loop for tensile testing of ASTM D638 Type I specimens, varying raster angle and line distance across 90 specimens manufactured and tested without human specimen handling. The per-specimen handling cycle was 17 minutes (versus 9 minutes for a human researcher), but 24-hour continuous operation yielded a projected throughput of 21.1 specimens/day and 633/month versus 8.42/day and 252.6/month for human researchers working 8-hour shifts (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010). The robotic researcher positioned specimens on the UTM with average errors of 268 μm and 0.19°, compared to 0.74° angular error for human researchers (pqac-00000011). The main limitation was battery life (eight experimental cycles before manual recharging) and scheduling of multiple parallel tasks (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009).

**Perception-driven polymer laboratory (Hernández-del-Valle et al. 2026, ChemRxiv preprint, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1).** This non-peer-reviewed preprint describes a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot with a UR10 cobot workcell processing injection-molded Charpy specimens (not FFF-printed). It processed 190 specimens in 274 minutes (1 min 26 s average per specimen), with a recoverable-error rate of 1.05% (one grasp failure and one incomplete cut detected and corrected) and two additional undetected incomplete cuts (1.05%) (pqac-00000050). Telegram-based alerts and event-driven recovery reduced supervision to brief, occasional interventions, supporting a one-researcher-per-laboratory model rather than one-operator-per-instrument (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056).

### (3) Camera-Based Print Monitoring and Verification

The following table summarizes reported accuracies for defect detection with camera-based systems:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings: Spaghetti/stringing detection using DeepLabV3 with tailored ASPP modules reached 95% accuracy at optimal dilation rate (pqac-00000030). Multi-class defect classification (cracking, layer shift, off-platform, stringing, warping) with MobileNetV2 transfer learning achieved 97% overall accuracy, while EfficientNetB0 reached 87.7%, with confusion primarily between cracking and layer shifting (pqac-00000031). Extrusion flow-rate error detection using ResNet-18 with a global-shutter camera achieved 96.1% classification accuracy at both low and high print speeds. The DaR3D thesis system detected print slippage at 89.6% accuracy using webcam images with controlled lighting. The commercial Obico/Spaghetti Detective system uses YOLOv2 but no independently validated accuracy metric was located in peer-reviewed literature (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036).

For **plate-clear verification**, the BEAR system uses an arm-mounted camera to check whether the bed is clear before each print, followed by robotic scraper cleaning with photographic verification after each attempt, up to ten retries (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). No published false-clear rate or classification accuracy for this verification step was found.

**No peer-reviewed study was found that specifically addresses automatic dimensional measurement of printed specimens before testing using low-cost cameras**, although SmartLab uses a wrist camera for dimension measurement with a reported 268 μm positional accuracy at the UTM (pqac-00000011), and the perception-driven polymer lab uses YOLOv11 segmentation and ArUco-based pose estimation for specimen localization (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052).

### (4) Print Farms with Robotic Tending

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that reports quantitative throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, or cost-per-part for a robotically tended FFF print farm in comparison to a manual farm.** The FlexTrak thesis describes a modular system designed to attach one removal mechanism per printer, enabling queued production through OctoPrint on Raspberry Pis, with the goal of continuous operation requiring human intervention only for filament spool replacement every few days (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061). However, the planned reliability tests (overnight, weekend, and full-spool runs) were proposed rather than reported (pqac-00000061). Budzik et al. (2024) describe a conceptual robotic MEX cell in which a collaborative arm transfers platforms and parts but provide no measured farm-level metrics (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063). Post-processing is estimated to add approximately 17–100% to printing time and roughly 30% of manufacturing cost, with labor costs of approximately USD 30–100/hour (pqac-00000059). These figures suggest substantial economic incentive for automation but remain indirect comparisons rather than controlled farm studies. **This represents a clear gap in the published literature.**

### (5) Remote or Cloud Users Submitting Design-Print-Test Jobs

**SmartLab Tanzania pilot (2025):** Twenty-one students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania remotely conducted material-testing experiments on equipment hosted at Seoul National University in Korea. Students controlled the system via a GUI and monitored it through real-time 360° VR streaming; temporary network disconnections did not halt experiments, as recorded VR video could be replayed (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000068). Two full cycles of material testing were successfully completed remotely (pqac-00000068). The system tolerated unstable network conditions without significant interruption to experimental procedures (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). No numerical job-completion rate or turnaround-time distribution was reported.

**BEAR external-user pilot:** No measured outcomes (completion rate, turnaround, interventions) for external users submitting jobs to the BEAR system were found in the accessible published literature. The BEAR data are reportedly available through kablab.org/data (pqac-00000040), but no publication describing external-user pilot results was located.

**No other published cloud-lab design-print-test system with measured user outcomes was identified.** This area remains largely undocumented in the peer-reviewed literature.

### (6) Feasibility Analysis for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

**Adhesion forces.** Kaščak et al. (2024, *Applied Sciences*, DOI: 10.3390/app14020945) measured PETG tear-off force on a PEI-coated spring-steel build plate at 53.48 ± 7.95 N (mean ± SD over 12 trials), compared with 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminum (pqac-00000025). PLA was explicitly excluded from that study because it "generally adheres sufficiently to commonly used uncontaminated surfaces" (pqac-00000024). **No peer-reviewed measurement of PLA adhesion force on textured PEI was located**, representing a data gap. Higher bed temperature generally increases adhesion, with temperatures slightly above the glass-transition temperature recommended for first-layer bonding (pqac-00000026). PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA on aluminum substrates: 5.94 MPa vs. 3.92 MPa at their respective optimal conditions (pqac-00000029).

**Sheet-flexing forces.** The FlexTrak system measured approximately 15.48 N normal force to break Prusa MK3 magnetic bed retention and 6.76 N horizontal pull after the edge was lifted (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). This is well within the PiPER arm's 15 N gripper force specification, but the arm's J5 ±70° wrist limitation would make straight-down grasps near the table infeasible. Sheet flexing was rated the most reliable removal method, requiring the least effort and posing minimal risk of part damage in a qualitative evaluation (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

**Feasibility for the PiPER arm on A1 mini bed-slingers.** The A1 mini is a bed-slinger (Y-axis moves the bed), which means the magnetic spring-steel sheet can in principle be slid off the bed by the arm. With approximately 15 N of gripping force, the PiPER could grip the sheet edge and pull it, since horizontal pull requires only about 6.76 N (pqac-00000015). However, the 53 N tear-off force for PETG on PEI significantly exceeds the arm's force budget, so direct scraping or perpendicular prying of well-adhered parts would likely fail. The recommended strategy for small PLA toys is: (a) allow cooling to room temperature (the BEAR system uses 30 °C for PLA removal; pqac-00000041), which substantially reduces adhesion on textured PEI; (b) slide the magnetic sheet off the bed (requiring <16 N; pqac-00000015); and (c) flex the sheet to pop parts free, as commercial flex plates "require the least effort" and are "reliable" with "minimal risk of part damage" (pqac-00000019). The ±70° J5 limitation means the arm should approach the bed edge laterally rather than from directly above.

**Grasping irregular printed parts.** No study specifically examining parallel-gripper grasping of irregular 3D-printed parts was found. General robotic grasping literature reports that underactuated grippers achieve 90–98% success rates on mixed-object benchmarks, and CNN-based grasp planners on parallel grippers can handle unknown objects including those with irregular shapes. For the specific case of small printed toys, compliant or soft-padded parallel jaw inserts would improve grasp stability. ### (1) Academic and Industrial Systems for Robotic Part Removal from FFF/FDM Printers

The following table compares all identified systems:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

**BEAR / MAMA BEAR (Boston University).** The Bayesian Experimental Autonomous Researcher (BEAR), first reported in Gongora et al. 2020 (*Science Advances*, DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aaz1708), uses five dual-extruder MakerGear M3 FDM printers arranged within the working radius of a six-axis Universal Robots UR5e arm, a Sartorius CP225D scale, and an Instron 5965 universal testing machine (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000002). The expanded campaign (Snapp et al. 2024, *Nature Communications*, DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48534-4) details the removal method: before each print, an arm-mounted camera checks whether the bed is clear; if cleaning is needed, the arm uses a scraper with up to ten retry attempts, taking a verification photo each time; if the bed remains dirty the printer is deactivated and an operator is notified (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). After printing, the bed is heated for TPE and TPU-1/2 (100 °C) to facilitate removal, or allowed to cool to 30 °C for PLA, PETG, Nylon, and TPU-3 (pqac-00000041). Failure modes include dirty beds, unsuccessful component grabs, misorientation, mass/height deviations >5%, severe print defects, insufficient strain data, and periodic need to replace worn polyimide tape and load new filament rolls (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). No explicit handling success-rate percentage was reported.

**FlexTrak automated sheet-flexing system (thesis, 2020).** This non-peer-reviewed student project describes a modular system for the Prusa i3 MK3 that elevates the magnetic spring-steel sheet off the bed (requiring approximately 15.48 N normal force to break magnetic retention, and 6.76 N horizontal pull), feeds it through a curved bending track using powered rollers, and uses passive scrapers to remove remaining debris (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016). A decision-matrix comparison rated sheet flexing higher than disposable roll media (3.75 vs. 3.1) for reliability, modularity, and maintainability (pqac-00000018). Scraper-only removal was tested and found unreliable: it damaged small parts, retained parts on the blade, was limited to about 38% of the bed area (150 cm² maximum on a 400 cm² bed), required favorable part orientation and rafts, and produced visible scrape marks after 250 cycles (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022). Print-head collision/ejection was also described, wherein modified G-code causes the print head to ram the part off; this requires no hardware modification but needs parts approximately 1 inch tall and becomes harder as contact area increases (pqac-00000017). Overnight, weekend, and full-spool reliability tests were planned but not quantitatively reported (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061).

**ATCAM (Mazhari et al. 2021, *Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance*, DOI: 10.1007/s11665-021-06042-2).** This peer-reviewed system prints dynamic coupons on a Prusa MK3S and ejects them using an in-situ actuator (ISA) printed on the build surface; the toolhead pulls back the ISA, which releases stored energy through a 25.4 mm sphere to impact-eject each coupon toward a load cell (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). The actuator generates approximately 2 N of force, and the coupon base is designed with reduced contact area to lower adhesion. Each ISA was reused for 100 nondestructive ejection cycles, after which manual replacement was required (pqac-00000045). A total of 3,000 coupons were generated across three PLA feedstocks (pqac-00000048). No explicit ejection success rate was reported, but automated ejection was described as the most difficult engineering challenge (pqac-00000044).

**SmartLab (Yun et al. 2025, *Journal of Computational Design and Engineering*, DOI: 10.1093/jcde/qwaf034).** This peer-reviewed system uses a San Robotics M1013 arm on a Syscon Scorpion A-100 mobile base. After printing, the robot removes the entire printer bed with a suction gripper, measures the specimen with a wrist camera, changes to a finger gripper via a pneumatic gripper changer, detaches the specimen, and places it on a rack for downstream measurement and testing (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000012). No bed temperature or cool-down protocol was specified in the retrieved evidence.

**Commercial systems.** Prusa Research's automated farm system (Prusa Pro AFS) and other commercial plate-swapping solutions (e.g., Bambu Lab conveyor concepts) exist as trade products, but **no peer-reviewed trial counts, success rates, failure-mode studies, or comparative cost analyses were located.** These should be treated as commercial/trade sources only.

### (2) Closed-Loop Design-Print-Test Systems with Robotic Specimen Handling

**BEAR (2020) and MAMA BEAR / expanded campaign (2024)** are the most extensively documented systems. BEAR demonstrated fully autonomous closed-loop operation: Bayesian optimization selected a structure design, OpenSCAD generated the STL, Slic3r produced G-code, OctoPrint managed the printer, the UR5e retrieved the part, weighed it, loaded it into the Instron 5965, and the compression test result fed back into Gaussian-process regression to guide the next experiment (pqac-00000004). In the original campaign, 600 designs were tested in triplicate without human intervention; 32 experiments in 12 hours matched a 1,800-experiment grid campaign, and 64 experiments in 24 hours exceeded it (pqac-00000006). The expanded campaign reported 25,387 experiments across seven materials (TPE, TPU-1/NinjaFlex, TPU-2/Cheetah, TPU-3/Armadillo, Nylon, PETG, PLA), with experiments running approximately 60% of wall-clock time and each mechanical test taking approximately 10 minutes (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000039). This directly contradicts any claim that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop. Human interventions included periodic manual bed cleaning when automated scraping failed after ten attempts, filament replacement, and polyimide tape maintenance (pqac-00000038). The authors state limitations including manufacturing variability (mass CV 4.6%, toughness CV 12.8%) and the need for human monitoring to modify campaign parameters during the multi-year operation (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000040).

**SmartLab (2025)** demonstrated a closed loop for tensile testing of ASTM D638 Type I specimens, varying raster angle and line distance across 90 specimens manufactured and tested without human specimen handling. The per-specimen handling cycle was 17 minutes (versus 9 minutes for a human researcher), but 24-hour continuous operation yielded a projected throughput of 21.1 specimens/day and 633/month versus 8.42/day and 252.6/month for human researchers working 8-hour shifts (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000010). The robotic researcher positioned specimens on the UTM with average errors of 268 μm and 0.19°, compared to 0.74° angular error for human researchers (pqac-00000011). The main limitation was battery life (eight experimental cycles before manual recharging) and scheduling of multiple parallel tasks (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009).

**Perception-driven polymer laboratory (Hernández-del-Valle et al. 2026, ChemRxiv preprint, DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1).** This non-peer-reviewed preprint describes a TurtleBot 4 mobile robot with a UR10 cobot workcell processing injection-molded Charpy specimens (not FFF-printed). It processed 190 specimens in 274 minutes (1 min 26 s average per specimen), with a recoverable-error rate of 1.05% (one grasp failure and one incomplete cut detected and corrected) and two additional undetected incomplete cuts (1.05%) (pqac-00000050). Telegram-based alerts and event-driven recovery reduced supervision to brief, occasional interventions, supporting a one-researcher-per-laboratory model rather than one-operator-per-instrument (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056).

### (3) Camera-Based Print Monitoring and Verification

The following table summarizes reported accuracies for defect detection with camera-based systems:

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

Key findings: Spaghetti/stringing detection using DeepLabV3 with tailored ASPP modules reached 95% accuracy at optimal dilation rate (pqac-00000030). Multi-class defect classification (cracking, layer shift, off-platform, stringing, warping) with MobileNetV2 transfer learning achieved 97% overall accuracy, while EfficientNetB0 reached 87.7%, with confusion primarily between cracking and layer shifting (pqac-00000031). Extrusion flow-rate error detection using ResNet-18 with a global-shutter camera achieved 96.1% classification accuracy at both low and high print speeds. The DaR3D thesis system detected print slippage at 89.6% accuracy using webcam images with controlled lighting. The commercial Obico/Spaghetti Detective system uses YOLOv2 but no independently validated accuracy metric was located in peer-reviewed literature (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036).

For **plate-clear verification**, the BEAR system uses an arm-mounted camera to check whether the bed is clear before each print, followed by robotic scraper cleaning with photographic verification after each attempt, up to ten retries (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000038). No published false-clear rate or classification accuracy for this verification step was found.

**No peer-reviewed study was found that specifically addresses automatic dimensional measurement of printed specimens before testing using low-cost cameras**, although SmartLab uses a wrist camera for dimension measurement with a reported 268 μm positional accuracy at the UTM (pqac-00000011), and the perception-driven polymer lab uses YOLOv11 segmentation and ArUco-based pose estimation for specimen localization (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052).

### (4) Print Farms with Robotic Tending

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that reports quantitative throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, or cost-per-part for a robotically tended FFF print farm in comparison to a manual farm.** The FlexTrak thesis describes a modular system designed to attach one removal mechanism per printer, enabling queued production through OctoPrint on Raspberry Pis, with the goal of continuous operation requiring human intervention only for filament spool replacement every few days (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061). However, the planned reliability tests (overnight, weekend, and full-spool runs) were proposed rather than reported (pqac-00000061). Budzik et al. (2024) describe a conceptual robotic MEX cell in which a collaborative arm transfers platforms and parts but provide no measured farm-level metrics (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063). Post-processing is estimated to add approximately 17–100% to printing time and roughly 30% of manufacturing cost, with labor costs of approximately USD 30–100/hour (pqac-00000059). These figures suggest substantial economic incentive for automation but remain indirect comparisons rather than controlled farm studies. **This represents a clear gap in the published literature.**

### (5) Remote or Cloud Users Submitting Design-Print-Test Jobs

**SmartLab Tanzania pilot (2025):** Twenty-one students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania remotely conducted material-testing experiments on equipment hosted at Seoul National University in Korea. Students controlled the system via a GUI and monitored it through real-time 360° VR streaming; temporary network disconnections did not halt experiments, as recorded VR video could be replayed (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000068). Two full cycles of material testing were successfully completed remotely (pqac-00000068). The system tolerated unstable network conditions without significant interruption to experimental procedures (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067). No numerical job-completion rate or turnaround-time distribution was reported.

**BEAR external-user pilot:** No measured outcomes (completion rate, turnaround, interventions) for external users submitting jobs to the BEAR system were found in the accessible published literature. The BEAR data are reportedly available through kablab.org/data (pqac-00000040), but no publication describing external-user pilot results was located.

**No other published cloud-lab design-print-test system with measured user outcomes was identified.** This area remains largely undocumented in the peer-reviewed literature.

**Adhesion forces.** Kaščak et al. (2024, *Applied Sciences*, DOI: 10.3390/app14020945) measured PETG tear-off force on a PEI-coated spring-steel build plate at 53.48 ± 7.95 N (mean ± SD over 12 trials), compared with 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminum (pqac-00000025). Higher bed temperature generally increases adhesion, with temperatures slightly above the glass-transition temperature recommended for first-layer bonding (pqac-00000026). PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA on aluminum substrates: 5.94 MPa vs. 3.92 MPa at their respective optimal conditions (pqac-00000029).

This is well within the PiPER arm's 15 N gripper force specification, but the arm's J5 ±70° wrist limitation would make straight-down grasps near the table infeasible. The 1.5 kg payload of the PiPER arm is well above the mass of small PLA toys (typically <50 g) but would limit handling of multiple parts simultaneously or large fixtures.

Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, roughly 15 N of gripping force, wrist joint J5 limited to plus or minus 70 degrees, so no straight-down grasps near the table), SO-101 leader/follower arms, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, and Bambu Lab printers (two A1 mini bed-slingers with 180 mm magnetic textured-PEI plates, and an H2D). Prints are sent remotely by an AI agent after a human approval, and the agent will not send a print until a camera frame shows the plate clear; today a person removes every part. We want the arm to clear plates (first for a batch of small toys on the A1 minis in December), and later to move printed specimens into mechanical tests inside closed design-print-test loops: 3D-printed tensegrity structures under drop or compression tests, and printed fixtures for our alloy and powder workflows. A previous literature answer claimed that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop; we believe Boston University's BEAR and MAMA BEAR systems (Gongora et al. 2020, Science Advances; Snapp et al. 2024, Nature Communications) contradict this, and we also know of SmartLab (2025), TeleopLab, and commercial plate-swapping systems such as Prusa's automatic sheet changer.

Question.
(1) Which academic and industrial systems use a robot arm (or other mechanism) to remove parts from FFF/FDM printers or swap build plates? For each: the removal method (flexing a magnetic spring-steel sheet, scraping or pushing, swapping the whole plate, tilting, ejection by the print head), the printers and arms used (especially any low-cost arms), measured success rates with trial counts, cycle times, failure modes (parts stuck when warm, small or tall parts tipping, adhesion changes with plate wear), and the bed temperature or cool-down conditions that make release reliable.
(2) Closed-loop design-print-test systems with robotic specimen handling (BEAR and MAMA BEAR, SmartLab, and any others): what the arm does, how specimens reach testing machines (universal testers, compression, impact or drop rigs), throughput, uptime, human interventions or failure rates reported, and the limitations and future work their authors state.
(3) Camera-based print monitoring and verification relevant to a robot cell: detecting print failures (detachment, spaghetti, warping, layer shift) with low-cost cameras and reported accuracy; checking that the plate is clear before the next print; and automatic measurement of printed specimens (dimensions, mass, defects) before testing.
(4) Print farms with robotic tending: published throughput, uptime, human hours per print and cost per part, versus manual farms.
(5) Remote or cloud users who submit design-print-test jobs (for example BEAR's external-user pilots or teleoperated test labs): measured outcomes such as completion rate, turnaround and interventions.
(6) Given our arm's limits, which removal methods are feasible for small parts on a 180 mm bed-slinger, what forces are involved (adhesion force of PLA or PETG on textured PEI, sheet-flex force), and what is known about grasping irregular printed parts with a parallel gripper?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints, theses, and commercial or trade sources. For each claim give the DOI or URL and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
