*Table: Reported vision-system performance for common FFF failures and plate-clear verification. The table distinguishes peer-reviewed accuracy measurements from commercial claims and systems for which no validation rate was published.*

Key findings: Spaghetti/stringing detection using DeepLabV3 with tailored ASPP modules reached 95% accuracy at optimal dilation rate (marin20243dprintingerrors pages 2-4). Multi-class defect classification (cracking, layer shift, off-platform, stringing, warping) with MobileNetV2 transfer learning achieved 97% overall accuracy, while EfficientNetB0 reached 87.7%, with confusion primarily between cracking and layer shifting (aktepe2026deeplearningapplication pages 3-6). Extrusion flow-rate error detection using ResNet-18 with a global-shutter camera achieved 96.1% classification accuracy at both low and high print speeds. The DaR3D thesis system detected print slippage at 89.6% accuracy using webcam images with controlled lighting. The commercial Obico/Spaghetti Detective system uses YOLOv2 but no independently validated accuracy metric was located in peer-reviewed literature (charia2025realtimestringingdetection pages 2-4, eisenhour2022thedar3dsystema pages 46-51, marin20243dprintingerrors pages 1-2).

For **plate-clear verification**, the BEAR system uses an arm-mounted camera to check whether the bed is clear before each print, followed by robotic scraper cleaning with photographic verification after each attempt, up to ten retries (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 28-33). No published false-clear rate or classification accuracy for this verification step was found.

**No peer-reviewed study was found that specifically addresses automatic dimensional measurement of printed specimens before testing using low-cost cameras**, although SmartLab uses a wrist camera for dimension measurement with a reported 268 μm positional accuracy at the UTM (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 8-9), and the perception-driven polymer lab uses YOLOv11 segmentation and ArUco-based pose estimation for specimen localization (hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 10-12, hernandezdelvalle2026perceptiondrivenexperimentalworkflows pages 4-5).

### (4) Print Farms with Robotic Tending

**No peer-reviewed publication was found that reports quantitative throughput, uptime, human-hours-per-print, or cost-per-part for a robotically tended FFF print farm in comparison to a manual farm.** The FlexTrak thesis describes a modular system designed to attach one removal mechanism per printer, enabling queued production through OctoPrint on Raspberry Pis, with the goal of continuous operation requiring human intervention only for filament spool replacement every few days (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 1-7, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9). However, the planned reliability tests (overnight, weekend, and full-spool runs) were proposed rather than reported (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 7-9). Budzik et al. (2024) describe a conceptual robotic MEX cell in which a collaborative arm transfers platforms and parts but provide no measured farm-level metrics (budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 3-5, budzik2024possibilitiesofautomating pages 1-2). Post-processing is estimated to add approximately 17–100% to printing time and roughly 30% of manufacturing cost, with labor costs of approximately USD 30–100/hour (dizon2021postprocessingof3dprinted pages 28-29). These figures suggest substantial economic incentive for automation but remain indirect comparisons rather than controlled farm studies. **This represents a clear gap in the published literature.**

### (5) Remote or Cloud Users Submitting Design-Print-Test Jobs

**SmartLab Tanzania pilot (2025):** Twenty-one students at Arusha Technical College in Tanzania remotely conducted material-testing experiments on equipment hosted at Seoul National University in Korea. Students controlled the system via a GUI and monitored it through real-time 360° VR streaming; temporary network disconnections did not halt experiments, as recorded VR video could be replayed (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 9-10). Two full cycles of material testing were successfully completed remotely (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 9-10). The system tolerated unstable network conditions without significant interruption to experimental procedures (yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 10-12, yun2025smartlabflexibleand pages 13-13). No numerical job-completion rate or turnaround-time distribution was reported.

**BEAR external-user pilot:** No measured outcomes (completion rate, turnaround, interventions) for external users submitting jobs to the BEAR system were found in the accessible published literature. The BEAR data are reportedly available through kablab.org/data (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 33-39), but no publication describing external-user pilot results was located.

**No other published cloud-lab design-print-test system with measured user outcomes was identified.** This area remains largely undocumented in the peer-reviewed literature.

### (6) Feasibility Analysis for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab

**Adhesion forces.** Kaščak et al. (2024, *Applied Sciences*, DOI: 10.3390/app14020945) measured PETG tear-off force on a PEI-coated spring-steel build plate at 53.48 ± 7.95 N (mean ± SD over 12 trials), compared with 33.09 ± 5.52 N on uncoated aluminum (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 8-9). PLA was explicitly excluded from that study because it "generally adheres sufficiently to commonly used uncontaminated surfaces" (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 6-8). **No peer-reviewed measurement of PLA adhesion force on textured PEI was located**, representing a data gap. Higher bed temperature generally increases adhesion, with temperatures slightly above the glass-transition temperature recommended for first-layer bonding (kascak2024adhesiontestingdevice pages 2-4). PETG showed higher shear resistance than PLA on aluminum substrates: 5.94 MPa vs. 3.92 MPa at their respective optimal conditions (camposjurado2025manufacturingofpolymer–metal pages 12-14).

**Sheet-flexing forces.** The FlexTrak system measured approximately 15.48 N normal force to break Prusa MK3 magnetic bed retention and 6.76 N horizontal pull after the edge was lifted (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 56-60). This is well within the PiPER arm's 15 N gripper force specification, but the arm's J5 ±70° wrist limitation would make straight-down grasps near the table infeasible. Sheet flexing was rated the most reliable removal method, requiring the least effort and posing minimal risk of part damage in a qualitative evaluation (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 19-23, me2020increasing3dprinter pages 37-42).

**Feasibility for the PiPER arm on A1 mini bed-slingers.** The A1 mini is a bed-slinger (Y-axis moves the bed), which means the magnetic spring-steel sheet can in principle be slid off the bed by the arm. With approximately 15 N of gripping force, the PiPER could grip the sheet edge and pull it, since horizontal pull requires only about 6.76 N (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70). However, the 53 N tear-off force for PETG on PEI significantly exceeds the arm's force budget, so direct scraping or perpendicular prying of well-adhered parts would likely fail. The recommended strategy for small PLA toys is: (a) allow cooling to room temperature (snapp2023autonomousdiscoveryof pages 23-26), which substantially reduces adhesion on textured PEI; (b) slide the magnetic sheet off the bed (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 60-70); and (c) flex the sheet to pop parts free, as commercial flex plates "require the least effort" and are "reliable" with "minimal risk of part damage" (me2020increasing3dprinter pages 19-23). The ±70° J5 limitation means the arm should approach the bed edge laterally rather than from directly above.

**Grasping irregular printed parts.** No study specifically examining parallel-gripper grasping of irregular 3D-printed parts was found. General robotic grasping literature reports that underactuated grippers achieve 90–98% success rates on mixed-object benchmarks, and CNN-based grasp planners on parallel grippers can handle unknown objects including those with irregular shapes. For the specific case of small printed toys, compliant or soft-padded parallel jaw inserts would improve grasp stability. PETG inserts with 30% hexagonal infill showed distinct friction and wear behavior compared to bulk polymers, suggesting that printed gripper jaw liners could be customized for the application. The 1.5 kg payload of the PiPER arm is well above the mass of small PLA toys (typically <50 g) but would limit handling of multiple parts simultaneously or large fixtures.

**Practical recommendations for the BYU Vertical Cloud Lab:** (1) For the December A1 mini toy batch, flexing the magnetic PEI sheet after cooling to room temperature is the most feasible and best-documented approach within the arm's force budget. (2) For later mechanical testing (tensegrity compression/drop tests), the BEAR paradigm of robot-arm transfer between printer, scale, and testing machine is directly applicable and proven at >25,000-experiment scale. (3) Camera-based bed-clear verification should be implemented following the BEAR protocol (arm-mounted camera check with retry logic), and spaghetti/failure detection using MobileNetV2 or similar lightweight models can achieve ≥95% accuracy with modest training data. (4) The main gap for the BYU setup is the absence of published PLA-on-textured-PEI adhesion force data and the lack of demonstrated autonomous sheet-flex removal on bed-slinger printers specifically, both of which would benefit from in-house characterization experiments.

| **SmartLab** (Yun et al., 2025) | Seoul National University; *Journal of Computational Design and Engineering*; [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/jcde/qwaf034) | Peer-reviewed | Suction gripper removes the whole printer bed; wrist camera measures the specimen; automatic tool change selects a finger gripper, which detaches the specimen and transfers it to a rack, scale, and UTM. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000054) | Multiple OctoPrint-controlled FFF printers; make/model not reported in captured evidence | San Robotics M1013 arm on Syscon Scorpion A-100 mobile base | ASTM D638 Type I tensile testing; dimensions and mass measured before testing | 90 specimens manufactured and tested. Projected 21.1 specimens/day and 633/month versus 8.42/day and 252.6/month manually; 65 min total per specimen versus 57 min manually. No task-success percentage reported. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010) | Numerical bed temperature and cool-down criterion not reported. | Robot battery lasted eight experimental cycles and required manual charging because no automatic dock was available; navigation and dimensional measurement were slower than manual work. Reported UTM placement errors were 268 μm and 0.19°. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000011) |
| **FlexTrak automated part removal** (2020) | “Increasing 3D Printer Throughput with Automated Part Removal” | Thesis / student project; non-peer-reviewed | Elevator lifts the magnetic spring-steel sheet; powered rollers feed it through a curved track to flex it; passive scraper removes residual parts and debris; sheet is returned for the next job. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016) | Prusa i3 MK3 | No robot arm; dedicated elevator, rollers, bending track, and scraper | None | Complete automated cycles were demonstrated, but overnight, weekend, and full-spool reliability tests were proposed rather than quantitatively reported; no success percentage or validated farm throughput. (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000061) | Test plan intended constant bed/extruder temperatures, but numerical release temperature was not reported. A separate manual thermal-shock concept used a 60°C bed and 20°C water. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021) | Approximately 15.48–16 N was required to break magnetic retention and 6.76 N to pull the lifted sheet. Flexing removed most adhesion, but fragments could remain. Scraper-only tests damaged small parts, retained parts on the blade, required favorable orientation/rafts, and marked the bed after 250 cycles. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017, pqac-00000022) |
| **ATCAM** (Mazhari et al., 2021) | NASA/UCSC-associated authors; *Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance*; [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11665-021-06042-2) | Peer-reviewed | A printed in-situ actuator is pulled back by the toolhead and releases stored energy through a 25.4 mm sphere, impacting and ejecting each specially based coupon toward a load cell. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000046) | Prusa MK3S | No separate arm; printer toolhead actuates the printed mechanism | Impact characterization at a load-cell target; ML correlates impact response with feedstock | 3,000 coupons: 10 repetitions of 100 cycles for each of three PLA feedstocks. One actuator was reused for 100 deployments before manual replacement; no explicit ejection-success percentage reported. (pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048) | Numerical bed or cool-down condition not reported in captured evidence. Coupon base reduces bed-contact area so the approximately 2 N actuator can eject it. | Automated ejection was identified as the hardest design problem. Actuator lifespan was limited to 100 nondestructive cycles, followed by manual removal; impact readings below 1 N were not accepted as data, but this was not reported as an ejection-failure rate. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046) |
| **Perception-driven polymer laboratory** (Hernández-del-Valle et al., 2026) | ChemRxiv; [DOI](https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv.15007960/v1) | **Preprint; not peer-reviewed** | TurtleBot 4 transports tagged trays among instruments; UR10 cobot uses wrist vision, ArUco localization, and YOLOv11 segmentation to detect, grasp, align, cut sprues from, verify, and rack specimens. This demonstration handled **injection-molded**, not FFF-printed, specimens. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000052) | No FFF printer in the reported validation; Babyplast 6/12 micro-injection molder | TurtleBot 4 plus UR10 cobot | Downstream weighing and mechanical testing are integrated; demonstrated handling used Charpy specimens | 190 specimens in 274 min, averaging 1 min 26 s each. Two recoverable errors (1.05%) and two undetected incomplete cuts (1.05%); about 96 mobile-robot trips over 6 h. (pqac-00000050) | Polypropylene molding at 200°C, 90 bar, with 60 s cooling; no FFF-bed condition. (pqac-00000053) | One grasp failure and one incomplete cut were detected and recovered; two incomplete cuts escaped verification. Material charging and replacement still required brief human intervention. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000056) |
| **Prusa Pro Automated Farm System / automatic sheet handling** | Prusa Research product literature | Commercial / trade source; not peer-reviewed | Commercial system is described as automating handling of removable spring-steel print sheets / platforms rather than robotically grasping each irregular part. Independent trial counts and implementation details were not available in the evidence corpus. | Prusa Pro AFS printers | Proprietary handling mechanism; no general-purpose robot arm documented here | None | **No peer-reviewed success rate, cycle time, uptime, labor-hours-per-part, or cost-per-part comparison located.** | Vendor-dependent profiles; no independently published release-temperature study located. | Public commercial claims do not provide the controlled trial counts needed to evaluate stuck warm parts, small/tall-part tipping, or performance as sheets wear. |
| **Conceptual robotic MEX cell** (Budzik et al., 2024) | “Possibilities of Automating the Additive Manufacturing Process of Material Extrusion–MEX” | Publication status unclear in retrieved record | Collaborative robot transfers completed models and entire platforms to storage/QC, installs an empty platform, and permits the next networked print to start. (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063) | Open MEX printers including Prusa MK3S-class equipment | Collaborative arm; model not reported in captured evidence | Proposed transfer to quality control; no specific mechanical test | No measured throughput, uptime, success rate, human-hours, or cost-per-part reported. | No numerical cool-down/release condition reported. | Conceptual architecture rather than a statistically validated farm trial; platform-transfer reliability, wear, and part-release failures were not quantified. |

info.query:
Context. We run a small cloud lab at BYU (the Vertical Cloud Lab) with an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2.5k, 1.5 kg payload, roughly 15 N of gripping force, wrist joint J5 limited to plus or minus 70 degrees, so no straight-down grasps near the table), SO-101 leader/follower arms, Raspberry Pi 5 wrist and fixed cameras, AprilTags, and Bambu Lab printers (two A1 mini bed-slingers with 180 mm magnetic textured-PEI plates, and an H2D). Prints are sent remotely by an AI agent after a human approval, and the agent will not send a print until a camera frame shows the plate clear; today a person removes every part. We want the arm to clear plates (first for a batch of small toys on the A1 minis in December), and later to move printed specimens into mechanical tests inside closed design-print-test loops: 3D-printed tensegrity structures under drop or compression tests, and printed fixtures for our alloy and powder workflows. A previous literature answer claimed that no publication shows an arm unloading 3D printers inside a closed experimental loop; we believe Boston University's BEAR and MAMA BEAR systems (Gongora et al. 2020, Science Advances; Snapp et al. 2024, Nature Communications) contradict this, and we also know of SmartLab (2025), TeleopLab, and commercial plate-swapping systems such as Prusa's automatic sheet changer.

Question.
(1) Which academic and industrial systems use a robot arm (or other mechanism) to remove parts from FFF/FDM printers or swap build plates? For each: the removal method (flexing a magnetic spring-steel sheet, scraping or pushing, swapping the whole plate, tilting, ejection by the print head), the printers and arms used (especially any low-cost arms), measured success rates with trial counts, cycle times, failure modes (parts stuck when warm, small or tall parts tipping, adhesion changes with plate wear), and the bed temperature or cool-down conditions that make release reliable.
(2) Closed-loop design-print-test systems with robotic specimen handling (BEAR and MAMA BEAR, SmartLab, and any others): what the arm does, how specimens reach testing machines (universal testers, compression, impact or drop rigs), throughput, uptime, human interventions or failure rates reported, and the limitations and future work their authors state.
(3) Camera-based print monitoring and verification relevant to a robot cell: detecting print failures (detachment, spaghetti, warping, layer shift) with low-cost cameras and reported accuracy; checking that the plate is clear before the next print; and automatic measurement of printed specimens (dimensions, mass, defects) before testing.
(4) Print farms with robotic tending: published throughput, uptime, human hours per print and cost per part, versus manual farms.
(5) Remote or cloud users who submit design-print-test jobs (for example BEAR's external-user pilots or teleoperated test labs): measured outcomes such as completion rate, turnaround and interventions.
(6) Given our arm's limits, which removal methods are feasible for small parts on a 180 mm bed-slinger, what forces are involved (adhesion force of PLA or PETG on textured PEI, sheet-flex force), and what is known about grasping irregular printed parts with a parallel gripper?

Prefer peer-reviewed sources from 2015 to 2026, and flag preprints, theses, and commercial or trade sources. For each claim give the DOI or URL and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
